summary: Defines class extensions to PPP over AAL2 that give functionality similar to Multi Class Multi Link PPP over a single ATM virtual circuit. Instead of Multi Link PPP fragmentation, it relies on features of AAL2 itself.

plainLanguage.summary: Some data, like voice, is urgent, and some can wait. These extensions let one connection sort messages into lanes by urgency without using extra tricks.

subtitle: Letting urgent voice fragments cut in front of bulk data on a single low-speed ATM circuit, using only what AAL2 already provides.

tldr.problem: On a slow ATM virtual circuit, one large data packet can block small real-time packets such as voice for a long time, which makes interactive use painful.
tldr.mechanism: Each PPP packet is classified into a preemption class, fragmented by the SSSAR sublayer, and each class is sent on its own AAL2 CPS Channel ID so the CPS layer can schedule urgent fragments between less urgent ones.
tldr.outcome: It gives roughly what Multi Class Multi Link PPP gives, without Multi Link PPP, by reusing machinery PPP over AAL2 already requires.

facts.label: Example delay
facts.value: about 100 ms for 1500 bytes at 128 kbit/s

today: RFC 3337 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2002. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3337 extends RFC 3336, which defines how a PPP session is carried over an ATM virtual circuit using AAL2. AAL2 is described as a bandwidth-efficient way to carry IP applications that generate small packets, with RTP-encapsulated voice (Voice over IP) as the example.

The document defines a set of class extensions to PPP over AAL2 that implement equivalent functionality to Multi Class Multi Link PPP over a single ATM virtual circuit. It uses the Segmentation and Reassembly Service Specific Convergence Sublayer (SSSAR) rather than Multi Link PPP for fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Some messages, like a phone call, are small and urgent. This document explains how to keep them from getting stuck behind big, slow ones on the same connection.

sections.title: Why Real-Time Traffic Needs Preemption
sections.content:
Real-time applications such as voice need low latency. RFC 2689 describes an architecture for real-time services on low bit rate links, and it calls for a real-time encapsulation format that guarantees low latency in the presence of large non real-time packets.

The RFC gives a concrete case: a 1500 byte packet on a 128 kbit/s ATM virtual circuit makes the link unavailable for real-time information for about 100 ms. That adds a worst-case delay that makes round-trip times too high for many interactive tasks.

Multi Class Multi Link PPP solves this by extending Multi Link PPP (RFC 1990) so a sender can fragment packets of various priorities into classes of fragments and send high-priority ones between fragments of lower priorities. RFC 3337 gets the same effect a different way. For the general service requirements it simply points to section 2 of RFC 2686.
sections.plainLanguage: A big truck on a narrow road takes about a tenth of a second to pass. That is a long wait if you are in the middle of a phone call, so the small urgent things need a way to slip past.

sections.title: Classes Mapped to AAL2 Channel IDs
sections.content:
PPP over AAL2 already uses the SSSAR sublayer to segment PPP packets into frames that the AAL2 CPS can carry. SSSAR uses different AAL2 UUI code-points to say whether a segment is the last one of a packet, and it fragments all packets into 64 byte fragments.

The AAL2 CPS layer also has a Channel ID that identifies multiple streams of packets within one ATM virtual circuit. This document uses the Channel ID to identify the preemption class a fragment belongs to. Fragments from each class MUST be assigned to different Channel IDs, and each PPP session MUST have at least as many Channel IDs as there are different classes of preemptible traffic.

Packets must be classified as they are fragmented. Many classification methods may be used, and the architecture in RFC 2689 describes alternatives that MAY be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of message gets its own colored lane. Because the lanes are separate, the system can tell at a glance which pieces are urgent.

sections.title: Scheduling Fragments
sections.content:
Once each class has its own Channel ID, the AAL2 CPS layer can schedule fragments from the different classes. The AAL2 CPS specification does not say how to schedule payloads from different Channel IDs, so the method depends on the real-time needs of the applications.

Some real-time applications MAY require a priority-based CID scheduler, while others may only need a fair or weighted fair one. Implementations SHOULD implement AAL2 CPS CID schedulers that meet the requirements of multi-class real-time applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic controller decides whose turn it is. Depending on the job, the controller can always let the ambulance go first, or just make sure every lane gets a fair turn.

sections.title: Example: Voice and Data on One Circuit
sections.content:
The RFC's example carries both voice and non-voice packets over a low bandwidth virtual circuit. The circuit must be provisioned with a real-time traffic class such as VBRnrt or VBRrt. Two classes are enough, so the PPP over AAL2 session runs across 2 Channel IDs: one for large data packets and one for real-time voice.

Packets arriving at the PPP interface are first classified, and a simple classifier is packet size. Large packets go to the data class and small packets go to the real-time class. The size threshold may vary with the application and the circuit's transmission rate.

A separate instance of SSSAR fragmentation runs on each of the 2 Channel IDs, and the fragments are then scheduled onto the circuit by the AAL2 CPS layer. Most AAL2 SAR implementations are said to use fair scheduling across Channel IDs, so a real-time fragment waits for at most one non-real-time fragment before being scheduled.
sections.plainLanguage: Small packets, like voice, go in the fast lane and big ones go in the slow lane. A voice packet never waits for more than one slow-lane piece.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is a single sentence: operation of this protocol is believed to be no more and no less secure than operation of PPP over AAL2 (RFC 3336). It adds no new security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding lanes does not make the road any safer or less safe than it already was.
